dimension_grades.evidence: The letter contains no phrases like 'passionate about,' 'results-driven,' or similar motivational filler; the closest is 'one of my favorite problems to work on,' which is conversational rather than motivational.
The writer never uses generic adjectives like 'dynamic,' 'innovative,' or 'strategic leader' — self-description is done through narrated actions and decisions.

Every positive claim is backed by specifics: the claim about following evidence to uncomfortable conclusions is supported by the detailed story of killing a 40,000 MAU feature; sequencing discipline is supported by the description of managing three domains with eleven engineers.

Key sentences like 'The last product I killed had 40,000 monthly active users' and the specific details about Cerro Systems and Ridgeline could not be copy-pasted into another applicant's letter without rewriting.
The letter avoids slang, exclamation points, and sentence fragments used for effect; the tone is conversational but structured throughout.
The letter avoids stiff formality — it opens with a specific anecdote rather than 'I am writing to express my interest,' and never uses phrases like 'I would be honored' or 'please find enclosed.'
Sentences vary significantly in length and structure, from short ('It was also the right call.') to complex multi-clause sentences, creating a natural reading rhythm.
Accomplishments are stated directly ('22% improvement in net revenue retention,' 'shipped in five months instead of twelve') without hedging or boasting, letting the facts speak.

Multiple quantified outcomes are included: '22% improvement in net revenue retention,' 'data pipeline latency from roughly four hours to under twenty minutes,' 'shipped in five months instead of twelve.'

Methods are described: 'I spent my first three weeks interviewing sixteen customers,' 'cohort analysis told a different story,' 'built the case for sunsetting it, redirected the three-person team toward an integration layer.'
Constraints are explicitly mentioned: 'a shared engineering team of eleven,' 'three-person team,' 'companies in the 150–600 employee range,' 'not enough headcount to run parallel bets on everything.'
Proof points are woven into two extended narratives (the Cerro sunsetting story and the Ridgeline reporting module story) rather than presented as bullet points.

The closing references the company's specific stage: 'you've built strong initial traction and you're now at the point where the next layer of growth probably depends less on new feature volume and more on how well the existing surface area holds together.'
'I have some specific thoughts on how the onboarding experience could evolve to support that' hints at a concrete idea without fully delivering it, creating a curiosity gap.
The hook is grounded in a substantive product observation about the tension between new user expectations and power user behavior, which feels relevant and earned rather than forced.
The letter ends with 'I'd welcome the chance to get into the details,' which is a generic availability statement serving as the final impression.
'The last product I killed had 40,000 monthly active users' opens with a specific experience rather than a statement of intent to apply.
The opening is attention-getting but earned — the provocative first line is immediately grounded by 'It was also the right call' and a detailed factual account, rather than straining for drama.

By the end of the first paragraph, the reader understands the writer makes evidence-based product decisions, can manage team redirection, and has delivered measurable business outcomes (22% NRR improvement).
